The sources disagree on whether Delhi's hottest days are getting hotter. NASA POWER shows a clear fall, ERA5 shows no clear change, and the NOAA station shows a clear rise.

NASA POWER (MERRA-2): clearly going down by 0.25 °C per decade (95% range -0.47 to -0.04), January 1981 to December 2025.

ERA5 reanalysis via Open-Meteo archive: no clear change, 0.13 °C per decade (95% range -0.02 to 0.27), January 1981 to December 2025.

NOAA NCEI GHCN-Daily: clearly going up by 0.25 °C per decade (95% range 0.11 to 0.38), January 1981 to July 2025.

Sources: NASA POWER (https://power.larc.nasa.gov/), ERA5 via Open-Meteo (https://open-meteo.com/), and NOAA NCEI GHCN-Daily (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/). The first two use grid cells about 50 km and 25 km wide, while the NOAA figures come from one station, New Delhi Safdarjun, about 3 km from the point checked. Each monthly value is the hottest single day of that month, and station records have gaps.

answer:
The water stored on and in the land across Punjab and Haryana has clearly been decreasing. The satellites show a fall of 40.32 cm of water per decade (95% range -42.73 to -37.87 cm), from April 2002 to June 2026. That is about 40 cm less water every 10 years, as a layer spread over the region. A change this steady would be very unlikely if nothing were really changing.

Source: NASA GSFC GRACE and GRACE-FO mascons, https://earth.gsfc.nasa.gov/geo/data/grace-mascons

Caveats: each value covers an area a few hundred kilometres wide. The total includes soil moisture, snow and surface water, so groundwater alone cannot be isolated. Data are missing from mid-2017 to mid-2018.

NOAA CO-OPS has no tide gauge within 100 km of this point, so the nearest PSMSL gauge was used.

meaning.headline: Sea level here has clearly been rising.
meaning.limit: This is what tide gauges have already measured. It cannot tell you how high the sea will get.
